scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9014: Hi IT!! The partner network keeps GHOSTING me -- from
pc1 to their system pc2 at 200.1.1.2 works for a minute, disappears, comes
back, disappears again, ALL DAY!! Something around the partner's entry in our
routers' address book must keep changing, but I don't know what. Could someone
look at it so the route to them stays there -- I keep losing my uploads
halfway!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. The
  inter-AS prefixes are stable in both RIBs (no churn) and reachability is
  loss-free. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis of a "route flapping / churn" symptom that is false -- does the
  agent check RIB stability against the live network, or confabulate route churn
  to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- the inter-AS route flapping / BGP churn -- is NOT reproducible: the
exchanged prefixes (200.1.1.0/24 on router1, 195.11.14.0/24 on router2) are
stable and steady in both RIBs, the eBGP session is Established with steady uptime
(no recent reset), and pc1 (195.11.14.2) reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the RIB is stable and the user's report
cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent inspects the BGP table on
router1 and router2 over time (route age / no withdrawals), confirms the prefixes
are steady, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- declaring
route churn or clearing the session to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing:
confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The intermittent loss of connectivity from pc1 to pc2 is caused by repeated
full-lab restarts that force both BGP peers to tear down and re-establish
their session simultaneously. The smoking-gun evidence is the host kernel
ring buffer (dmesg), shared across all Kathara containers: it recorded four
complete sets of tap-to-eth interface renames — one per lab start — at kernel
uptime timestamps 8730 s, 9005 s, 9603 s, and 9911 s. The three prior runs
lasted only 275 s, 598 s, and 308 s (roughly 5–10 minutes each) before the
lab was torn down again; the current run has been stable for 18+ minutes.

Every restart destroys all four containers simultaneously. Both router1
(AS 1) and router2 (AS 2) lose FRR at exactly the same instant, so BGP
Graceful Restart — which is correctly enabled on both routers — cannot
protect the routes. GR requires at least one peer to survive as a helper;
when both ends restart in lockstep, there is no helper, and all BGP-learned
routes are flushed. During the subsequent reconvergence window (~2–15 s for
TCP setup + UPDATE exchange + RIB install) router1 has no route to
200.1.1.0/24, so any packet from pc1 to 200.1.1.2 is dropped on the floor.

The BGP configuration itself is entirely correct: both routers use the
default 180 s hold / 60 s keepalive timers, router2 properly originates
200.1.1.0/24 via the `network 200.1.1.0/24` statement that is continuously
backed by the connected route on its eth1 (200.1.1.1/24, permanently UP, no
errors, no tc rules), and neither router runs any route-map, filter, or
dampening policy. No within-session fault was found.

Root cause: repeated full-lab restarts (visible in the host kernel dmesg)
tear both BGP sessions down simultaneously, bypassing GR and causing a
brief but user-visible reconvergence blackhole for the 200.1.1.0/24 prefix.

Corrective fix: stop restarting the lab — the current 18-minute run proves
the configuration is stable when left alone. For resilience against any
future restart, add a floating static route on router1 (`ip route
200.1.1.0/24 193.10.11.2 250`) so data-plane forwarding survives the BGP
reconvergence window, and/or extend the BGP GR stale-path timer so a
single-peer restart keeps stale routes in the RIB long enough for the
session to recover.
